prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators

statement.case_for: Topological insulators remain, in my view, the strongest condensed-matter case on the table: five of seven colleagues who ranked B004 placed it in their top three or just outside, and all seven independently proposed the same trio. Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the spin-orbit-driven quantum spin Hall phase, a new symmetry-protected state of matter that cannot be adiabatically connected to an ordinary insulator. Molenkamp's group then measured the conductance quantisation of the helical edge channels in HgTe/CdTe wells in 2007, which is exactly the sequence of surprising theory followed by a decisive, quantitative experiment that I look for. Nearly two decades of independent confirmation (InAs/GaSb, Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 by ARPES, and a large body of ab initio materials prediction that my own community relies on) make this a mature and reproducible result. It is also a concept that quantum mechanics keeps delivering: band theory, once thought to be fully understood, turned out to hide a topological classification.
statement.case_against: The attribution is genuinely untidy. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp realised, Shoucheng Zhang can no longer be recognised, and Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and Hasan's group were decisive for the three-dimensional phase. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter is close enough that some will argue this is an incremental step. A prize for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would be defensible but leaves visible gaps, and I should not pretend that a clean three-name solution exists.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B004 fourth, weighing it as outside his expertise and worrying that credit is contested around Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu-Kane-Mele, and that overlap with the 2016 prize makes this an incremental step.
responses.response: I take the attribution worry seriously but would answer it this way. The 2016 prize honoured Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz for topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall and Haldane chain physics, which are strongly correlated or magnetic-field-driven and have no time-reversal-symmetric analogue. Z2 topological insulators are a distinct, symmetry-protected class with their own experimental confirmation, so this is a new step rather than a repeat. On credit, the committee's usual practice is to recognise the decisive theory and the first decisive experiment, and Kane-Mele-Molenkamp does that cleanly; BHZ's contribution is real, but they proposed a material platform, and the quantisation measured by Molenkamp was the experimental proof. I agree that expert reports must test this.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B009 first and B004 second, praising the clean Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model followed by experiment, and noting timely recognition though the superconductivity mechanism is debated, while flagging the overlap of B004 with 2016.
responses.response: I share Mehlig's appreciation for the Bistritzer-MacDonald model and ranked it second myself, but I differ on maturity. Topological insulators have been confirmed by independent groups for more than fifteen years across several material families, whereas the origin of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is still open and the field is about eight years old. I would not rule out B009, and I would support it if the committee wants a younger prize, but I judge that the robustness of the experimental picture currently favours B004. I would also ask whether Dean, Young and Yacoby on the experimental side are as indispensable as Jarillo-Herrero before settling on three names.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first and cold-atom quantum simulation second, arguing both are mature and stable, and partly deferred to condensed-matter colleagues on B004.
responses.response: I accept that B023 and B015 are mature and consequential, and I can follow the argument that quantum simulation is overdue. My reservation is that for B023 five credited names cannot be reduced to three without leaving out decisive theory or experiment, and for B015 Wallraff's omission is a real gap in a three-name prize, as Lindroth also notes. B004's attribution is awkward but its core, theory plus first experiment, fits in three names. I also note that the 2025 prize recognised superconducting circuits, so B015 might look like a close successor, which weighs on timing.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first as a clean precision-measurement result with a natural two-person credit, independently confirmed at 10^-18 in many laboratories and timely.
responses.response: I agree that B006 is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and exceptionally well reproduced, which is why I ranked it fifth and keep it as an alternative. My hesitation is not rigour but the type of discovery: the prize would recognise a superb measurement technology whose fundamental physics payoff (variation of constants, dark matter, redefinition of the second) is still pending. I would not object strongly if colleagues prefer it, but I would like the committee to weigh whether a new state of matter should take priority over a better ruler when both are mature.

uncertainties: Whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, or Fu and Moore, should be credited alongside or instead of one of the three named laureates, and whether expert reports would shift the balance.
Whether the committee views the 2016 topological prize as too close to B004 to repeat the subject so soon.
Whether the experimental credit for twisted bilayer graphene (Cao, Dean, Young, Yacoby) would need to be resolved before B009 can be considered mature enough.
How much weight to give measurement-technology prizes such as B006 versus discovery of a new state of matter.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted ballot. My field is first-principles theory of magnetism, adjacent to topological and moire materials, but I have no stated personal or institutional tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Katori or Ye.
